item.title: Microsoft-owned GitHub spotlighted a PS5-to-PC translation layer amid GTA 6 DMCA strikes, then quietly deleted the post
item.itunes:title: Microsoft-owned GitHub spotlighted a PS5-to-PC translation layer amid GTA 6 DMCA strikes, then quietly deleted the post
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
In a very odd move, Microsoft-owned GitHub's official Twitter account posted about AnyPS5, the most notable PlayStation 5-to-PC translation layer currently in development, celebrating its 58,000 stars since its August launch, while also highlighting the launch of GTA 6 and the efforts to bring the game unofficially to PC. Unsurprisingly, the post — which also included a well-put-together vertical video — was quickly deleted.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

GitHub's post arrived just after a DMCA takedown notice from Take-Two Interactive, the parent company of GTA 6 developer Rockstar, tied to a prominent GTA 6 porting effort, Lenoida and 3,007 related repositories. CGBJ, another notable GTA 6 PC port project that managed to get the game running between 25-30fps, also mysteriously disappeared this morning (it's unclear if Rockstar also hit the project with a DMCA).

It's unclear why GitHub posted about the ongoing efforts to get PlayStation 5 games playing on Windows PCs, while also celebrating the efforts to get GTA 6 running on PC, especially given the legal backlash from Rockstar that's already brewing. My best guess is the post came from a social media manager who didn't fully understand the situation.

The account has been posting influencer-style vertical videos for a few weeks now, but none seem to have crossed the line into highlighting the more legally dubious projects on GitHub. On top of that, Microsoft owns GitHub, and Sony owns the PlayStation 5 — it's really just all-around weird.

AnyPS5 is one of the leading efforts to bring PS5 games to PC

It's unclear if the tool will play a role in porting the PS5 version of GTA 6 to PC

Credit: Rockstar

Unlike traditional console emulators, AnyPS5 converts PS5 executables into native Windows and Linux programs, replacing the console's proprietary system libraries with its own open-source implementations. It's unclear if AnyPS5 will play a significant role in the efforts to get GTA 6 running on PC ahead of an official release.

Current GTA 6 PC port efforts are based on a leaked copy of the Xbox version of the game that appeared online earlier this week courtesy of Cyberleek, the same individual or group behind leaks surrounding the game from earlier this year. Cyberleek first released the game's files, followed by the executable developers need to port the Xbox version to PC. More recently, reports emerged that the PS5 version of GTA 6 has also leaked.

While GTA 6 is now available on the PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, Rockstar hasn't announced an official PC version yet. Rumors point to an official PC port launching somewhere between six months and a year from now. The relentless efforts to unofficially bring the game to PC might encourage Rockstar to launch its inevitable PC port early.

The leading unofficial GTA 6 PC port vanished from GitHub just as it reached a playable 25-30fps

Did Rockstar hit CGBJ with a DMCA? It's still unclear.

1
By  Patrick O'Rourke

item.title: Your old laptop is a great home server, but most people get these two things wrong
item.itunes:title: Your old laptop is a great home server, but most people get these two things wrong
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
With the RAM apocalypse in full swing, I’ve spent the last couple of months repurposing any and all hardware I could find into home servers for my tinkering experiments. Contrary to what many folks believe, you don’t need a top-tier processor or ungodly amounts of RAM to tinker with virtual machines and containers. As long as you’ve got an x86 system released in the last two decade, you can build a rock-solid self-hosting workstation without spending thousands of dollars.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

This statement also applies to laptops, and I say that as someone still using a budget Lenovo model from 2014 as a cluster node. If anything, laptops have a couple of advantages over traditional PCs for your tinkering experiments, provided you don’t fall into the same beginner traps when reusing your old daily driver as a container-hosting server.

My outdated Windows 10 PC was headed for the recycling bin until Proxmox gave it a second life

This dinosaur machine now runs my LLMs inside an LXC

4
By  Ayush Pande

Even an outdated laptop can host plenty of productivity tools

Yes, I speak from experience

On the surface, a dinosaur laptop may not seem all that impressive for server tasks, especially when you compare it to a tower-sized PC. That said, if all you’re planning to do is run a few containerized tools, even the cheapest laptops on flea markets can pull their own weight.

Heck, I’ve got a Lenovo G510 that can handle around ten FOSS tools, which is pretty darn impressive considering it’s powered by a mere 2-core processor and 4GB of RAM. Meanwhile, my Acer Predator Helios 300 has enough firepower to not only run a Windows 11 VM, but it can also drive AI models like Gemma 4 E4B at well over 30 tokens/second – at the same time, no less.

In fact, this i7-7700HQ machine can still double as a reliable remote gaming server for indie titles in 2026, and as long as I don’t go too trigger-happy when over-provisioning the system resources, I can even use it as a testing ground for my distro-hopping experiments. Proxmox works really well with old laptops, as its lightweight web UI doesn’t consume too many resources all while letting me tinker with GPU passthrough, clustering, and other advanced features.

But the laptops themselves have a couple of neat perks. Troubleshooting, for one, is a lot easier on my laptops, as I can use its built-in screen and keyboard to run different tests instead of scurrying around the house looking for displays and KB+M on my tower-sized PC servers. Even my outdated machines don’t consume too much energy when idle, which is far from their PC counterparts.

Plus, the fact that I can get Wi-Fi and Bluetooth provisions baked into my DIY workstation is pretty handy for Home Assistant and other services that can make use of wireless connectivity options. Sadly, I can’t quite say the same about my laptop batteries …

In the name of all that’s holy, its battery is not a UPS replacement

It’s more of a potential fire hazard

Many beginners treat the laptop battery as a stand-in for a dedicated UPS, which makes sense considering you could lose entire projects to a random outage. But one quick trip to the r/spicypillows subreddit is all it’d take to make you fear the built-in battery as much as I do.

Most laptops use lithium-ion batteries, and leaving them plugged in at 100% capacity non-stop can put them under a lot of chemical stress. Combine that with a home server that you’d end up running 24/7, and your laptop’s battery can end up degrading at an accelerated rate. Over time, it might start to swell up, at which point it becomes a potential fire hazard.

Personally, I prefer getting rid of the battery altogether, as I’d rather not deal with a ticking health hazard in my home lab nodes. But since many laptops don’t work without a battery shoved into their chassis, I use an automation pipeline to cap the maximum charging capacity on the battery.

Specifically, I’ve installed a Glances server directly on the Proxmox node to keep tabs on the battery statistics. Home Assistant already has a Glances integration, which makes importing the battery metrics a cakewalk. Toss a smart plug between the wall socket and the laptop’s charger, and all it takes is two automations to get this pipeline working – one that turns the smart plug off at a specific battery level (say, 80%), and another that turns it back on once the battery percentage hits the red zone.

I’d still recommend tossing the battery out of the laptop’s chassis whenever possible, but this wacky automation workflow can reduce the degradation rate to some extent.

I'm addicted to installing Proxmox on old devices

Proxmox has become my favorite virtualization platform for revitalizing outdated systems

8
By  Ayush Pande

Running your laptop with its lid closed isn’t a good idea, either

All that trapped heat can damage the chassis

Another laptop server “trick” I’ve seen floating around online is that keeping the lid closed can keep the keyboard dust-free and make it easy to pile up other hardware for an efficient-looking desk. Unfortunately, these perks come at steep costs, namely increased heat buildup and potential damage to the display and keyboard.

Plenty of laptops have air vents around the hinges and the top deck of the laptop, and you’ll find just as many that dissipate heat through the keyboard. Closing the lid can make these vents and openings inaccessible, thereby increasing the temps on your laptop. If you leave your laptop-turned-home server running 24/7, the extra heat would not only cause the laptop internals to start throttling, but could end up damaging the built-in screen and keyboard.

Your laptop can be a reliable home server, as long as you do things the right way

I’ve been using my dinosaur gaming and budget laptops as server nodes for well over a year now, and they’ve held up just fine during this time. Sure, they may not be as powerful as my repurposed Xeon workstation or an old 2K gaming PC. But thanks to Proxmox and a little bit of tinkering, they’re chugging along nicely as LXC-hosting rigs.

item.title: I replaced Google Drive and iCloud with a self-hosted Vaultwarden and Immich stack, and my monthly SaaS bill dropped to zero
item.itunes:title: I replaced Google Drive and iCloud with a self-hosted Vaultwarden and Immich stack, and my monthly SaaS bill dropped to zero
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Monthly subscriptions can start to add up. With a 2TB Google One plan at $9.99 per month paired with a 2TB iCloud Plus tier at $9.99 per month, you're already spending $20 a month (or $240 a year) just to keep photos synced and credentials accessible across devices without even considering optional Bitwarden Premium subscriptions. I got fed up and was experiencing a lot of subscription fatigue.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

So I decided to switch over to a self-hosted Vaultwarden and Immich stack. Immich handles mobile camera roll backups, media indexing, and shared albums, so I could replace Google Photos and iCloud Photos. Vaultwarden handled credential management, TOTP 2FA codes, and secure file attachments, replacing iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, and Bitwarden Premium. I implemented these tools by running them as containerized services via Docker Compose on my local NAS.

I'm torn between these 5 user-friendly NAS image hosting tools

Spoilt for choice

2
By  Chandraveer Mathur

Immich's UI is fantastic

I found the transition pretty seamless

Immich is a self-hosted open-source photo and video management platform. For me, it felt like a more privacy-focused alternative to my Google Photos and iCloud subscriptions because you run the server on your own hardware. You can use the mobile app or even the web interface to back up, browse, and organize your media. The UI is fantastic, and for me personally, it felt pretty indistinguishable from Google Photos. It syncs photos automatically from my iPhone, including live photos, and you get AI features like local facial recognition, object detection, and semantic search without sending your library to a third-party cloud.

When replacing Google Photos and iCloud Photos with Immich, the first thing to note is hardware sizing and resource consumption. Idle RAM usage is completely manageable, but the initial library ingestion (when it's generating thumbnails, transcoding videos, and running ML indexing across likely tens of thousands of assets) can spike CPU and memory usage. However, once you're past this, it runs pretty smoothly.

Once I had the container set up on my NAS, it was time to actually migrate everything. It was simple enough to export via Google Takeout and Apple's Privacy Portal and upload using Immich-Go, which preserved all of my timestamps, GPS coordinates, and album structures without creating any duplicate uploads. One thing I do want to note is that there was occasional friction with background sync throttling on iOS due to Apple's background task limit.

Password management was next on my list

And Vaultwarden was a great alternative

The next container installed was Vaultwarden for password management. It's an unofficial open-source server implementation of the Bitwarden API, written in Rust. It has a minimal footprint, easily running in a single container on less than 100MB of RAM with an embedded SQLite database, compared with the official Bitwarden self-hosted stack (which historically required a much heavier multi-container setup).

By self-hosting Vaultwarden while still using the official Bitwarden mobile apps, desktop clients, and browser extensions, you're able to access features that are typically locked behind Bitwarden's almost $20/year premium, such as built-in TOTP authenticator code generation, encrypted file attachments, emergency access, vault health reports, and multi-user organizations for household password sharing. These are all features that are available straight out of the box.

When you're trusting a self-hosted vault with primary credentials, there are some non-negotiable setup steps that you should undergo. HTTPS/TLS should be mandatory. Bitwarden clients rely on the Web Crypto API and refuse to authenticate over plain HTTP, so a reverse proxy with valid TLS certificates is mandatory, even on a local network.

You should never expose the admin panel or registration endpoints to the public internet. For an extra level of security, you can even keep the entire instance behind a split-horizon DNS and WireGuard/Tailscale mesh VPN so zero ports are forwarded to WAN altogether.

There are some caveats

Remote access requires some workarounds

There is a way to have remote access without implementing port forwarding, since the biggest practical hurdle of leaving iCloud and Google Drive is seamless syncing when you're away from your home Wi-Fi. There are two options here.

The first is a reverse proxy and public domain, which is what I opted for because it felt the most seamless for me. You can expose Vaultwarden and Immich over HTTPS (port 443) via Caddy or Nginx with Cloudflare DNS, which lets you share links with family members who aren't on your VPN.

If you've struggled to run your favorite childhood games on your modern PC, there's a very real reason. So many of these 2000s titles perform poorly on modern hardware because no official fixes were ever released. They might launch on your Windows 11 PC, but fail to support widescreen resolutions, lose mouse input, cut off audio in cutscenes, or break the physics beyond a certain framerate.

They would essentially be unplayable without community-made patches that fix nearly every game-breaking bug. Deus Ex (2000)

The one that started it all, in 2052

Credit: Steam

Until Aspyr announces a release date for the upcoming Deus Ex Remastered, the existing Deus Ex can be called anything but playable. The critically acclaimed cyberpunk RPG from 26 years ago is still regarded as one of the genre's defining games. I wish we could get the sequel to Deus Ex: Mankind Divided, but I digress. You should definitely play or revisit the original Deus Ex, but simply downloading it from Steam and installing it isn't enough.

Even if you want to avoid the popular "Revision" variant or the "GMDX" mod to retain the vanilla experience, you'll need at least the Deus Ex Maps Patch, Kentie's Launcher, and the OpenGL renderer. The maps patch fixes level issues left in the most recently patched version of the game, Kentie's Launcher makes it easy to dial in the right FPS and resolution settings for optimal stability, and OpenGL replaces the game's ancient default renderer to support modern Windows.

This guide makes it clear how to install each fix before you can enjoy the game. If community patches like these didn't exist, Deus Ex would not be a good experience on contemporary hardware.

Deus Ex (2000)

The one that started it all, in 2052

Credit: Steam

Until Aspyr announces a release date for the upcoming Deus Ex Remastered, the existing Deus Ex can be called anything but playable. The critically acclaimed cyberpunk RPG from 26 years ago is still regarded as one of the genre's defining games. I wish we could get the sequel to Deus Ex: Mankind Divided, but I digress. You should definitely play or revisit the original Deus Ex, but simply downloading it from Steam and installing it isn't enough.

Even if you want to avoid the popular "Revision" variant or the "GMDX" mod to retain the vanilla experience, you'll need at least the Deus Ex Maps Patch, Kentie's Launcher, and the OpenGL renderer. The maps patch fixes level issues left in the most recently patched version of the game, Kentie's Launcher makes it easy to dial in the right FPS and resolution settings for optimal stability, and OpenGL replaces the game's ancient default renderer to support modern Windows.

This guide makes it clear how to install each fix before you can enjoy the game. If community patches like these didn't exist, Deus Ex would not be a good experience on contemporary hardware.

item.itunes:summary:
I've been trying Android apps beyond the usual recommendations, and some turned out to be surprisingly useful. Not every great app needs to be popular or packed with flashy features. A few simply do everyday things better, while others add capabilities I didn't know my Pixel was missing. After experimenting with several options, these are five lesser-known apps that earned a permanent spot on my phone.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

StoryPad

Turns everyday notes into a personal timeline

StoryPad takes a different approach to note-taking and journaling. Instead of making me sort everything into folders, notebooks, or categories, it brings all my entries together in one chronological timeline. I can use the same space to jot down random thoughts, document my day, save memories, or work on longer pieces of writing. Each entry also supports rich-text formatting, checklists, photos, and multiple pages, making it useful for more than just quick diary entries.

My favorite part is the Throwbacks feature. It brings up entries written on the same date in previous years, giving me an easy way to revisit old memories and see what was happening in my life. StoryPad also tracks moods and lets me customize the appearance of my journal. My journal is stored locally by default, and I don't need an account to get started. It works offline, with optional Google Drive backup and manual syncing between devices.

StoryPad: My Daily Journal

DailyPad is an open-source journaling app that helps you capture daily thoughts, organize entries on a timeline, and maintain a private, offline-first journal without distractions or unnecessary features.

See at Google Play Store

Organic Maps

This offline maps app is a must-have for traveling

Organic Maps showed me how useful a dedicated offline navigation app can be. It uses OpenStreetMap data to provide detailed maps that I can download before heading out. Once the maps are saved, searching for addresses and places doesn't require an active internet connection. Turn-by-turn navigation works for driving, walking, and cycling, complete with voice guidance. I downloaded a map of my area and tested navigation with mobile data switched off.

It is also useful for exploring places beyond regular city roads. It includes hiking trails, cycling routes, mountain-bike paths, contour lines, and elevation profiles. It also lets you record GPS tracks and save favorite locations as bookmarks. I can even import and export routes in formats such as GPX and KML. The app is free, open source, and doesn't include ads, trackers, or mandatory registration. Having maps, search, and navigation available offline makes traveling through areas with poor connectivity much less stressful.

Organic Maps

Organic Maps is a free, open-source offline navigation app for Android and iPhone, offering privacy-focused, ad-free maps, hiking trails, driving directions, bookmarks, and maps without tracking users or collecting data.

See at Organic Maps

Ente Photos

A smarter way to manage photos without giving up privacy

I don't particularly like handing over my personal photo library just to get cloud backups. Ente Photos offers a more private alternative by encrypting photos and videos before uploading them, so even Ente cannot access their contents. It also preserves original image quality, making it a reliable way to back up memories without compression.

Beyond storage, Ente offers face recognition and Magic Search, which helps find pictures using descriptions such as a sunset, beach, or particular object. Both features use on-device machine learning, but need to be enabled in settings and take time to index photos backed up to Ente. You also get shared albums and curated memories, making it feel like a complete photo gallery rather than just a backup service. The free plan includes 10GB of storage, giving you enough room to try it before considering a paid subscription.

Ente Photos

Ente Photos is an open-source, end-to-end encrypted cloud storage and photo management app designed as a privacy-focused alternative to services like Google Photos and iCloud.

See at Ente Photos
I install these 5 open-source apps on every Pixel before anything else

A new Pixel is great out of the box, but these open-source apps make it even better.

3
By  Yash Patel

Blip

AirDrop-style file sharing works across platforms

Transferring files between my Pixel and Windows PC doesn't have to involve cloud storage or USB cables. Blip (free, non-commercial plan) is my go-to solution for file sharing. The best part is that Blip doesn't impose file-size limits or compress the files I send. After installing the app and signing in on both devices, I can select photos, videos, documents, or entire folders and send them to the recipient. The transfer doesn't require uploading everything to a cloud drive first and then downloading it again.

Blip's biggest advantage is that it has no file-size limits and preserves the original quality of photos and videos. It works across Android, Windows, macOS, Linux, and iOS, so I'm not restricted to transferring files between devices running the same operating system. Blip prefers direct connections over the local network or internet, but it can use encrypted server relays when a direct connection isn't possible. It also supports interrupted-transfer recovery, so a disrupted connection doesn't necessarily mean starting over.

Blip

Blip is a cross-platform file transfer app that lets you securely send files and folders directly between devices without cloud storage.

See at Official Website

Cashew

Tracking my spending no longer feels like a chore

I used to rely on spreadsheets to track expenses, which meant sorting through purchases whenever I wanted to understand my spending. Cashew makes this easier with a dedicated space for recording and organizing transactions. Adding a transaction takes just a few details, including its amount, account, and category. I can also create separate accounts for cash, bank balances, and credit cards to keep everything organized.

Cashew goes beyond basic expense tracking with flexible budgets, custom spending periods, and category-wise limits. Its visual reports use graphs and charts to show spending patterns and compare expenses over time. There are also savings goals, loans, and scheduled transactions for upcoming bills. I still have to record my transactions, but Cashew takes care of the calculations and reports, making it easier to see where my money goes.

Cashew

Cashew is a customizable expense and budget tracker app designed to help users log daily spending, manage budgets, and track financial goals without connecting bank passwords.

See at Google Play Store

You don't always need a new phone to enjoy a better Android experience. Sometimes, discovering the right apps is enough to make your existing device more useful. These five apps each bring something different to the table, and none feels like an unnecessary addition to my Pixel. It's always nice when a few lesser-known apps turn out to be the upgrades you didn't know you needed.

item.itunes:title: Turning off band steering fixed more Wi-Fi problems in my house than my mesh system did
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It's more of a common practice for homes to replace an aging ISP gateway or standalone router with a multi-node consumer mesh kit to eliminate dead zones around your home. While adding these mesh nodes will improve your signal bars across your rooms, it can sometimes fail to resolve underlying latency spikes, brief connection drops, IoT dropouts, and throughput stutters. This is because the bottleneck in many multi-node setups isn't a lack of RF coverage, but aggressive, opaque band steering (often branded as Smart Connect or Unified SSID Management) fighting against the client device's native roaming logic.

One of Wi-Fi 7's best features can actually slow your connection down

MLO is why Wi-Fi 7's speeds look incredible on paper, but real-world numbers are a bit more complicated

1
By  Ty Sherback

How does band steering work?

It might not be the right setting for your home

Under the IEEE 802.11 standard, roaming and band selection are strictly client-side decisions. Access points and mesh nodes don't have absolute control over which radio a phone, laptop, or smart plug can connect to. The client's wireless NIC and OS driver evaluate signal thresholds and then make the final choice.

Modern mesh systems use 802.11k to inform clients of nearby radios and then 802.11v to suggest moving from a congested 2.4 GHz radio to a 5GHz or 6GHz radio. However, these requests are advisory. Clients can ignore them, and most notably, iOS and macOS devices have strict RSSI delta requirements, such as requiring a stronger candidate signal before roaming, making them stick when sometimes it might not deliver the best performance.

When clients ignore 802.11v suggestions, many consumer routers fall back on non-standardized workarounds such as legacy steering tactics. These include probe response suppression, where they withhold 2.4 GHz probe responses so a dual-band client only sees the 5GHz BSS ID during scanning, and also forced deauthentication/disassociation frames in order to kick those sticky clients off of 2.4GHz.

This problem can be compounded by mesh systems too. In a single-router setup, a client only negotiates between two bands on one access point. In a three-node mesh system with tri-band or dual-band radios broadcasting a single unified SSID, a stationary client sits within earshot of six to nine distinct BSSIDs. Aggressive band steering combined with node steering creates competing transition requests across multiple BSSIDs simultaneously.

How did the band steering issue manifest in my home?

I was dealing with constant dropouts

When swapping over to a mesh system myself, I found quite a few different failure modes that I observed. The first was ping-ponging at coverage boundaries. Sometimes, this can be referred to as band flapping. This happens because 2.4GHz signals attenuate somewhat less through drywall, wood framing, and appliances than 5GHz or 6GHz signals. In rooms with moderate attenuation, a mesh node steering algorithm sees a dual-band client and pushes it onto 5GHz at -68 dBm. Once associated, packet error rates rise or the client's internal roam trigger (such as my iPhone's -70 dBm threshold) fires, dropping it back to the stronger 2.4GHz signal.

Five minutes later, the router's steering timer pushes my iPhone back to 5GHz again, and the cycle repeats. Each forced transition interrupts my browsing experience. Sometimes, it can be quick and unnoticeable, but sometimes it can be up to several seconds when full WPA2/WPA3 four-way handshakes are triggered.

I also found that a lot of my smart home devices, including plugs, thermostats, and security cameras, were using low-power 2.4GHz-only Wi-Fi chipsets. As a result, they lack 802.11v/r support. When a mesh node delays or suppresses 2.4GHz probe responses to prioritize 5GHz, these 2.4GHz-only clients experience scan timeouts, failed DHCP renewals, or persistent device offline states in companion apps.

Power transmission feels asymmetric when it comes to a lot of mesh nodes too. This is because consumer mesh kits frequently run both 2.4GHz and 5GHz radios at maximum default transmit power without manual power tuning. Because 2.4GHz propagates farther, clients moving through the house consistently hear the 2.4GHz beacon at a higher RSSI than 5GHz, causing client drivers to cling to 2.4GHz while the mesh controller repeatedly attempts to steer them off.

Disabling band steering changed everything

Splitting SSIDs made a difference too

I was able to fix this issue by disabling band steering and splitting my SSIDs. Turning off unified band steering (sometimes called Smart Connect, depending on your router's manufacturer) stopped my devices from being kicked off and steered to another BSSID. Separating the network into distinct SSIDs, specifically isolating a dedicated 2.4GHz SSID for IoT/legacy hardware while keeping high-throughput dual-band/tri-band clients on a dedicated 5GHz SSID.

This is what worked best for me. This was able to eliminate cross-band probe suppression, and the previous ping-ponging I was experiencing stopped, as stationary laptops and phones could lock onto 5GHz without dropping down to congested 20MHz channels on 2.4GHz.

Many entry-level consumer mesh systems don't expose toggles to disable band steering or split SSIDs, meaning you need to switch the mesh kit into bridge/access point mode behind a configurable router (or use prosumer access points that actually do allow this granular radio management).

When you are separating your SSIDs, there is a bit of a technical trade-off. 802.11v BSS transition management only operates within the same SSID/ESS, meaning a client on a 5GHz-only SSID will not automatically fall back to the 2.4GHz at the extreme edge of your home (where there might not be the correct coverage unless you manually switch).

I also decided to ensure that all of my mesh nodes used Ethernet as a backhaul where possible so that inter-node roaming didn't contend with client airtime.

Mesh systems may not solve all of your problems

Investing in a consumer mesh system will solve coverage problems like your signal strength across your square footage, but disabling flawed band steering solves stability problems because you're able to eliminate forced client disconnections and RF band flipping. Standards-based 802.11k/v steering can work reliably in well-tuned single-vendor environments with modern Wi-Fi 6/6E/7 clients and balanced transmit power, but on consumer mesh hardware with mixed IoT devices and thick interior walls, sometimes manual band separations remain the most predictable fix.

item.title: Someone built a Microsoft Office alternative for decades-old Atari computers, and it's delightfully retro
item.itunes:title: Someone built a Microsoft Office alternative for decades-old Atari computers, and it's delightfully retro
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • XL Office is free app suite for retro Atari 8-bit XL/CE PCs.
  • It includes XL Write, Calc, Paint, Show, Audio, and a browser — the whole suite is a 76KB download.
  • It's not practical, but offers up a welcome dose of nostalgia.

The team behind XL Office has dropped a suite of productivity tools for Atari's ancient 8-bit XL and CE PCs, which feature just 64KB of memory (via The Verge). The free collection includes a word processor, a drawing app, a browser, a spreadsheet, a PowerPoint alternative, and several more apps, all of which run on PAL and NTSC versions of the computers, as well as old-school Atari PC emulators.

On its website, XL Office lists several compatible Atari computer models, including the 1200XL (1982), the 130XE (1985), and the XEGS (1987). The company says that the original Atari 400 and 800 aren't supported because "they use a different operating system and lack the memory banking."

On the word-processing side, XL Office says XL Write features automatic word wrap, bold, italics, and underline. What more could you want from a word processor, right? XL Calc, the suite's delightfully retro-looking spreadsheet app, can handle sixteen columns and sixty-four rows, and includes formulas that recalculate as you type.

XL Show lets you create a simple presentation that looks like it's right out of 1987

Even if these retro Atari apps are vibe-coded, they're still undeniably cool

Credit: XL Office

My personal favorite app is the highly pixelated XL Show, XL Office's PowerPoint replacement. It lets you create 10 slides in one file and includes chart and full-screen support. Groundbreaking, right? There's also a cool-looking retro drawing app called XL Paint that gives me Windows 3.1 Paintbrush vibes, an audio-editing app called XL Audio, and even a retro web browser. If you want to see the retro office suite in action, there's a video up on XL Office's website.

None of these apps are very practical, obviously, but they're still pretty cool, particularly if you have an old 8-bit era Atari PC lying around. That said, I imagine most people interested in trying them will boot the apps through an XL and CE Atari emulator.

Amusingly, the download file for the entire XL Office 1.0 suite is only 76kb. It's unclear if the fun retro suite of office apps was entirely vibe-coded, but I wouldn't be surprised.

My GeForce RTX 4070 Ti Super has given me no room for complaints for about two years. It has handled both halves of my work during this time by driving my 1440p QD-OLED by delivering frame rates that justify its cost, and by running the large local models that I could've only dreamt of running on an 8GB graphics card. I have no plans to replace it, but if it died tomorrow and I had to buy a card for the same two jobs, I wouldn't buy a GeForce.

Nvidia's natural successor to my card is the RTX 5070 Ti, and the cheapest one in the US hit about $1,340 at the beginning of November. Bear in mind, that's the same card that launched at a recommended MSRP of $749, and it now costs about $340 more than the RTX 5080's launch price. In this dysfunctional market, though, none of the equivalent Blackwell cards retail at prices that a customer would find justifiable, and the only card that I would buy right now is the one that most would rule out for that kind of workflow without a second look.

The RX 9070 XT keeps pace with the 5070 Ti at 1440p

I wouldn't expect it to go neck-and-neck with RTX on ray tracing, though

item.title: I own a Kindle, Kobo and a Boox Palma, but this tiny e-reader won me over
item.itunes:title: I own a Kindle, Kobo and a Boox Palma, but this tiny e-reader won me over
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've now reached a weird stage where I seem to have tested more e-readers than books I've actually read in the past year. Testing a new one out always gives me a solid reason to read and call it work, but at this point, it takes quite a bit for an e-reader to genuinely excite me.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

After all, between my Kindle, Kobo, and Boox Palma, there isn't much I feel like I'm missing out on. Yet, of all the e-readers I've played around with, it's the smallest one I've ever tested that's managed to win me over: the Boox Picco.

None of my existing e-readers were letting me down

An already well-rounded collection

Before I begin talking about why I've grown so attached to the Picco, I wanted to preface this article by pointing out that I already had an e-reader for practically every use case I could think of. Whenever I wanted a pocket-friendly e-reader I could carry around without having to think twice, I'd reach for my Boox Palma. The fact that it runs Android also meant I wasn't tied to a particular bookstore or even a particular reading app.

My Kindle and Kobo, on the other hand, are both excellent at being what I think an e-reader should fundamentally be: a distraction-free device you can sit down and read on for hours. Whenever I'm traveling, I'm also more inclined to pack either my Kindle or Kobo than my Palma. They're both compact enough to slip into my carry-on without taking up much space, yet have comfortably sized displays that I can spend hours reading on during a long-haul flight.

As much as I appreciate the Palma's portability, its tall and narrow form factor can feel a little awkward at times, especially during longer reading sessions. It sometimes feels a bit too much like reading on my smartphone, which is precisely what I'm trying to get away from.

The Picco's form factor is easily my favorite thing about it

Practically attached at the hip (or phone)

As I mentioned earlier, portability has always been one of the things I've appreciated most about my Boox Palma. But as pocket-friendly as the Palma is, it still felt like an additional device I had to make a conscious effort to carry around. That's not something I can say about the Picco. With a 3.97-inch display, a thickness of just 5.5mm, and a weight of approximately 58 grams, there are times when I forget I have it on me!

My Picco also came with a MagSafe-compatible case, meaning I can simply attach it to the back of my iPhone and head out. Given that my phone goes practically everywhere with me anyway, so does my Picco now. Whether I'm heading to college or stepping out to run a quick errand, I don't necessarily need to anticipate having enough downtime to justify bringing an e-reader along. It's already there if I need it.

The Picco takes the best of all three worlds

A little bit of everything, literally

One of the things that initially caught me off guard about the Picco was that, unlike the vast majority of Boox's devices, it doesn't run Android. As much as I've appreciated having access to the Google Play Store on the other Boox devices I've tested, I don't miss it at all on the Picco.

Boox has included a handful of basic apps, including a Pomodoro timer (which I'm particularly fond of), a to-do list, a countdown timer, and an app to keep track of your reading stats. You'll also find an Images app, which I think is a tad unnecessary. That's pretty much it. There's very little you can do on the Picco that'll distract you from what you picked it up to do in the first place.

What's even better is that despite stripping away Android, Boox hasn't stripped away the freedom that comes with owning one of its e-readers. The Picco doesn't revolve around a particular bookstore, and transferring your own books onto the device is incredibly straightforward.

You can do so via a local network connection from your phone, through the cloud, or using a USB cable. I've primarily been using the Phone LAN Transfer option, which takes mere seconds once you've installed the Boox Tiles app on your phone. Boox also recently rolled out native EPUB support, so there's no need to convert your EPUB files to a proprietary format before reading them anymore.

In many ways, the Picco gives me the same freedom I've always appreciated about my Palma, while being just as intentional about keeping distractions to a minimum as my Kindle and Kobo.

The Picco makes it ridiculously easy to squeeze in a few pages

A few pages here, a few chapters there

What I really appreciate about the Picco is how easy it makes it to fit reading into my everyday schedule, which is something I've always struggled with. I've typically treated reading as an activity I need to actively set aside time for, whether that's an hour before bed or a quiet Sunday afternoon. More often than not, something else comes up, and I end up not reading at all.

With the Picco, I've found myself reading in little pockets of time I'd otherwise spend mindlessly scrolling through my phone. Whether I'm waiting for my next class to begin, grabbing a coffee, or waiting for someone to pick me up, it's incredibly easy to squeeze in a few pages. Since the Picco is so comfortable to hold and operate with one hand, I don't necessarily need to find somewhere to sit down and get comfortable to read, either.

Individually, these are all ridiculously short periods of time that I'd never have thought to dedicate to reading. But they add up surprisingly quickly throughout the day. For someone who's spent the better part of the past year trying to get back into the habit of reading regularly, that's made a much bigger difference than I would've anticipated.

With a 3.97-inch display, a thickness of just 5.5mm, and a weight of approximately 58 grams, there are times when I forget I have it on me!

My Picco also came with a MagSafe-compatible case, meaning I can simply attach it to the back of my iPhone and head out. Given that my phone goes practically everywhere with me anyway, so does my Picco now. Whether I'm heading to college or stepping out to run a quick errand, I don't necessarily need to anticipate having enough downtime to justify bringing an e-reader along. It's already there if I need it.

The Picco takes the best of all three worlds

A little bit of everything, literally

One of the things that initially caught me off guard about the Picco was that, unlike the vast majority of Boox's devices, it doesn't run Android. As much as I've appreciated having access to the Google Play Store on the other Boox devices I've tested, I don't miss it at all on the Picco.

Boox has included a handful of basic apps, including a Pomodoro timer (which I'm particularly fond of), a to-do list, a countdown timer, and an app to keep track of your reading stats. You'll also find an Images app, which I think is a tad unnecessary. That's pretty much it. There's very little you can do on the Picco that'll distract you from what you picked it up to do in the first place.

What's even better is that despite stripping away Android, Boox hasn't stripped away the freedom that comes with owning one of its e-readers. The Picco doesn't revolve around a particular bookstore, and transferring your own books onto the device is incredibly straightforward.

You can do so via a local network connection from your phone, through the cloud, or using a USB cable. I've primarily been using the Phone LAN Transfer option, which takes mere seconds once you've installed the Boox Tiles app on your phone. Boox also recently rolled out native EPUB support, so there's no need to convert your EPUB files to a proprietary format before reading them anymore.

In many ways, the Picco gives me the same freedom I've always appreciated about my Palma, while being just as intentional about keeping distractions to a minimum as my Kindle and Kobo.

The Picco makes it ridiculously easy to squeeze in a few pages

A few pages here, a few chapters there

What I really appreciate about the Picco is how easy it makes it to fit reading into my everyday schedule, which is something I've always struggled with. I've typically treated reading as an activity I need to actively set aside time for, whether that's an hour before bed or a quiet Sunday afternoon. More often than not, something else comes up, and I end up not reading at all.

With the Picco, I've found myself reading in little pockets of time I'd otherwise spend mindlessly scrolling through my phone. Whether I'm waiting for my next class to begin, grabbing a coffee, or waiting for someone to pick me up, it's incredibly easy to squeeze in a few pages. Since the Picco is so comfortable to hold and operate with one hand, I don't necessarily need to find somewhere to sit down and get comfortable to read, either.

Individually, these are all ridiculously short periods of time that I'd never have thought to dedicate to reading. But they add up surprisingly quickly throughout the day. For someone who's spent the better part of the past year trying to get back into the habit of reading regularly, that's made a much bigger difference than I would've anticipated.

item.itunes:summary:
If you've ever wondered whether your laptop is really charging, or why a file transfer is crawling, a hub that shows you the answer is easy to appreciate. The Anker USB-C Smart Display Hub puts a small screen right on the unit, and it's now $74.99 on Amazon for Black Friday, a $25 savings off its $99.99 regular price.

The Anker Nano 10-in-1 USB-C Hub is a desktop hub with a built-in 2-inch Smart Display that shows charging wattage, data speed and temperature. It has HDMI 2.1 and DisplayPort 1.4 outputs for two monitors, 10Gbps USB ports, and passes up to 80W to a laptop.

See at Amazon

A lot of utility for the money

Real-time stats and productivity tools

The standout feature is the 2-inch smart display, which shows your current charging wattage, data transfer speed, temperature status, and port occupancy. There's a physical button on the hub too. Beyond the stats, Anker built in a Pomodoro timer and focus reports, which are nice extras if you spend long days at your desk.

You get 10 ports in total. For video, there's one HDMI 2.1 port and one DisplayPort 1.4 port, alongside 1 Gbps Ethernet, SD and microSD card slots that support speeds up to 104 MB/s, and USB-C and USB-A data ports. Keep in mind that the USB-A ports and the front USB-C port are data-only, meaning they won't carry video or charging.

For monitors, a single display can run at up to 4K@144Hz, while two displays can hit 4K@120Hz or 2K@240Hz. Dual 2K@240Hz requires a laptop USB-C port with DP 2.1 and DSC 3:1. On Windows, two external monitors can show different content, but on macOS, both mirror the same content. USB-C monitors aren't supported, so plan on using the HDMI and DisplayPort outputs.

The rear USB-C PD-IN port accepts up to 100W and passes up to 80W to your laptop. With a 100W PD charger, the hub reserves 20W for itself. Anker recommends a 65W or higher charger, and one isn't included. If you don't already own one, factor in the cost.

Anker's page lists a magnetic base, a Velcro strap, and a 700mm upstream cable in the box, though it says that isn't a full contents list. The hub measures 5.12 × 1.97 × 2.19 in and weighs 11.64 oz. It works with Windows 10/11 and macOS, but it isn't compatible with Linux. If you run Linux or you rely on USB-C monitors, you should skip it. If you plan to run two high-refresh monitors, check your laptop's USB-C port specs first. For Windows and Mac users with HDMI or DisplayPort monitors, it's a good fit.

At $74.99, the hub matches its all-time low on Keepa, and we think that's a fair price for this many ports plus a screen that shows what's going on. You can grab the Anker USB-C Smart Display Hub on Amazon while the sale lasts.
